lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Histology is the study of tissues, so dissecting and analysing the heart points to a histologist.
  • Biometry uses statistics to answer questions such as how many people get lung cancer by smoking.
  • Al-Qanun fil-Tibb is the famous book of Bu Ali Sina.
  • Volvox has a large number of cells but shows colonial, not true multicellular, organisation.
  • In the five kingdom system, mushrooms belong to kingdom Fungi.
  • The heart of a frog represents the organ level of organisation.
  • Oxygen makes up most of the composition of an organism's body.

Correct answer: Organ

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Biophysics explains the working of the eye and ear, blood flow, and instruments like the microscope.
  • A biology student can adopt medicine and serve humanity by diagnosing and treating diseases.
  • The Holy Quran says: 'We made from water every living thing' (Surah Al-Anbiya, Ayah 30).
  • Jabir bin Hayyan introduced experimental chemistry and described many chemical processes.
  • Bu Ali Sina wrote Al-Qanun fil-Tibb and Ibn Nafees described the circulation of blood.
  • Volvox is a green alga whose hundreds of cells live together as a hollow ball-like colony.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers for the following questions

Q: i. How the understanding of physics can help the biologist?

Ans: Physics helps the biologist in understanding the physical processes of life. For example, the working of the eye and ear, the flow of blood under pressure, the lever action of bones and muscles, and the use of instruments like the microscope, X-rays and centrifugation are all explained by the principles of physics. This combined study is called biophysics.

Q: ii. Which career would you like to adopt after studying biology and why?

Ans: After studying biology I would like to adopt medicine as my career. A biology student can become a doctor and serve suffering humanity by diagnosing and treating diseases. (Any one career can be chosen, for example medicine, agriculture, horticulture, forestry, fisheries, animal husbandry or teaching, with its reason.)

Q: iii. Write the translation of any three verses of the Holy Quran related to the creation of mankind.

Ans: 1. "We made from water every living thing." (Surah Al-Anbiya, Ayah 30). 2. "Who made all things good which He created, and He began the creation of man from clay." (Surah Al-Sajda, Ayah 7). 3. "Verily We created man from a product of wet earth (clay)." (Surah Al-Muminoon, Ayah 12).

Q: iv. Name few Muslim Scientists and their contributions in the field of biology and medicine.

Ans: Jabir bin Hayyan introduced experimental chemistry and described many chemical processes. Bu Ali Sina (Avicenna) wrote the famous book Al-Qanun fil-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine). Abdul Malik Asmai wrote books on animals such as Al-Khail (horses) and Al-Ibl (camels). Ibn Nafees described the circulation of blood. Jabir bin Hayyan, Bu Ali Sina and other Muslim scientists laid the foundation of modern biology and medicine.

Q: v. What level of organization is represented by Volvox?

Ans: Volvox represents the colonial level of organization. It is a green alga in which hundreds of unicellular organisms live together in the form of a hollow ball-like colony. The cells are similar and each cell can live independently, so Volvox is not a true multicellular organism.

mcqs.why: The quoted verse says He began the creation of man from clay, and Surah Al-Muminoon, Ayah 12, likewise says man was created from a product of wet earth.

mcqs.why: The short answer credits Jabir bin Hayyan with introducing experimental chemistry and describing many chemical processes, while the other contributions belong to other scientists named there.

mcqs.why: The short answer says Abdul Malik Asmai wrote books on animals such as Al-Khail (horses) and Al-Ibl (camels), so Al-Khail is his book on horses.

options: The structure of the eye only
mcqs.why: The short answer on Muslim scientists states directly that Ibn Nafees described the circulation of blood, a major contribution to biology and medicine.

mcqs.why: The short answer says Volvox is a green alga in which hundreds of unicellular organisms live together in the form of a hollow ball-like colony.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Biogeography studies the distribution of organisms in space and time, such as kangaroos only in Australia.
  • Biochemistry explains the chemical composition of living bodies and processes like photosynthesis and respiration.
  • Biology comes from bios meaning life and logos meaning study.
  • Histology studies tissues, morphology the external form, and anatomy the internal structure.
  • Sixteen elements are bio-elements, and six of them make 99 percent of the mass of living organisms.
  • Robert Whittaker in 1969 classified living organisms into five kingdoms.
  • Phosphorus is a part of ATP, bones and nucleic acids.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers for the following questions

Q: i. How the understanding of biology can be improved through the knowledge of geography, chemistry and statistics? Give examples.

Ans: Biology is an inter-disciplinary science. Geography helps in biogeography, the study of the distribution of organisms in space and time, for example why kangaroos are found only in Australia and why malaria mosquitoes flourish in damp and warm areas. Chemistry explains the chemical composition of living bodies and processes like photosynthesis and respiration; this branch is biochemistry. Statistics, as biometry, is used to collect and analyse biological data, for example counting how many people get lung cancer by smoking or comparing the cost and profit of biological projects. Thus knowledge of these subjects makes the understanding of biology deeper and more exact.

Q: ii. Define biology. How can you describe your own body under different branches of biology?

Ans: Biology is the branch of science which deals with the study of life and living organisms. The word is derived from two Greek words: bios meaning life and logos meaning study. My own body can be described under different branches of biology: morphology describes its external form and structure; anatomy describes its internal structure; histology studies its tissues; physiology explains the functions of its organs; embryology describes its development before birth; genetics explains how characters passed into it from parents; and biochemistry explains the chemical processes going on inside its cells.

Q: iii. Enlist the various levels of biological organization and explain it with an example.

Ans: The levels of biological organization are: (1) Sub-atomic particles and atoms; (2) molecules and compounds, i.e. micromolecules and macromolecules; (3) organelles; (4) cells; (5) tissues; (6) organs; (7) organ systems; (8) organism; and above the organism level, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere. Example: in man, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms join to form glucose molecules; molecules make organelles such as mitochondria; organelles form a muscle cell; cells form muscle tissue; tissues make the heart (organ); the heart with blood vessels forms the blood circulatory system; and all systems together make the organism, man.

Q: iv. Explain the role of bio elements for living organisms.

Ans: About 92 elements occur naturally and 16 of them are called bio-elements because they take part in the composition of living organisms. Only six elements, oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium and phosphorus, make 99 percent of the total mass of living organisms. Oxygen is used in respiration and forms the largest part of the body; carbon is the backbone of all organic compounds; hydrogen is a part of water and organic molecules; nitrogen is essential for proteins and nucleic acids; phosphorus is a part of ATP, bones and nucleic acids; and calcium is needed for bones, teeth and blood clotting. Without these elements the structure and life processes of organisms would be impossible.

Q: v. Who classify the living organisms into five kingdom. Explain each kingdom with the living organisms included in it.

Ans: Robert Whittaker in 1969 classified all living organisms into five kingdoms. (1) Kingdom Prokaryotae (Monera): unicellular prokaryotic organisms without a membrane-bounded nucleus, e.g. bacteria and cyanobacteria. (2) Kingdom Protista or Protoctista: unicellular eukaryotic organisms, e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena and algae. (3) Kingdom Fungi: multicellular eukaryotic organisms whose cell wall is made of chitin; they are heterotrophic and absorb food, e.g. mushrooms, moulds and yeast. (4) Kingdom Plantae: multicellular eukaryotic autotrophic organisms which prepare their own food by photosynthesis, e.g. Brassica, mulberry and pine. (5) Kingdom Animalia: multicellular eukaryotic heterotrophic organisms without cell walls, e.g. jellyfish, worms, insects, fish, frog, birds and mammals including man.

mcqs.why: The detailed answer lists the levels in order: organelles, then cells, then tissues, then organs, then organ systems and then the organism.

mcqs.why: The detailed answer states phosphorus is a part of ATP, bones and nucleic acids, while calcium is needed for bones, teeth and blood clotting.

mcqs.why: The detailed answer states Robert Whittaker in 1969 classified all living organisms into five kingdoms: Prokaryotae, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Observations are the first step in the biological method.
  • A hypothesis must be consistent with data, testable, and able to make deductions; it need not be correct.
  • Deductions are made from a hypothesis.
  • The actual answer to a scientific problem is the conclusion.
  • Data from experiments are best analysed by applying statistical formulae.
  • Only the Anopheles mosquito can transmit Plasmodium in human beings.
  • Laveran first found Plasmodium in the blood of a malarial patient.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Encircle the best suitable answers

Q: i. Which one is the first step in biological method?

Options: (a) Hypothesis (b) Experiment (c) Observations (d) Deduction

Correct answer: Observations

Q: ii. What is the correct experiment to know that Plasmodium destroys red blood cells?

Options: (a) Examine the blood of a single healthy person (b) Examine the blood of a single infected person (c) Allow mosquito to bite a healthy person and examine his blood (d) Examine the blood of some healthy and also some infected persons

Correct answer: Examine the blood of some healthy and also some infected persons

Q: iii. What is the best way to analyse the data collected from experiments?

Options: (a) Reading the data and drawing conclusions (b) Discussion with scientists (c) Simple calculations on calculator (d) Application of statistical formulae

Correct answer: Application of statistical formulae

Q: iv. People who slept near smoky fire had less chance to suffer from malaria. Why?

Options: (a) Smoke kills Plasmodium in their blood (b) Fire increases temperature and Plasmodia are killed in air (c) Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled (d) Smoke kills Plasmodium present in mosquitoes

Correct answer: Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled

Q: v. Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of a hypothesis?

Options: (a) It must be consistent with all available data (b) It must be testable (c) It must be correct (d) Must make deductions

Correct answer: It must be correct

Q: vi. Deductions are made from:

Options: (a) Observations (b) Hypothesis (c) Experiment results (d) Solution of biological problem

Correct answer: Hypothesis

Q: vii. Which one of the following is true about the statement of hypothesis?

Options: (a) Logical (b) Possible answer (c) based upon observations (d) All of them

Correct answer: All of them

Q: viii. The actual answer to scientific problem is:

Options: (a) Observations (b) Hypothesis (c) Data (d) Conclusion

Correct answer: Conclusion

Q: ix. Which mosquito can transmit Plasmodium in human beings?

Options: (a) Anopheles (b) Culex (c) Aedes (d) All of these

Correct answer: Anopheles

Q: x. For the first time, who found Plasmodium in the blood of malarial patient?

Options: (a) Ronald Ross (b) Laveran (c) A. F. A. King (d) Mendel

Correct answer: Laveran

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Science is knowledge gained through observations and experiments about the natural world.
  • A control group is kept under normal conditions without the factor being tested.
  • Without a control group, no reliable conclusion can be drawn from an experiment.
  • One malaria deduction was that stopping mosquito bites should stop the spread of malaria.
  • Ronald Ross proved mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium by letting a mosquito bite a patient and then a healthy person.
  • A hypothesis is accepted or rejected at the stage of experimentation and analysis of results.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: i. What is a science? How does it work?

Ans: Science is the knowledge gained through observations and experiments about the natural world. It works through the scientific method: a problem is recognized, observations are made, a hypothesis is formed, deductions are drawn from it, and experiments are performed to test the hypothesis. If the results support the hypothesis it is accepted, otherwise it is rejected or modified.

Q: ii. Control group is important for scientific study, How?

Ans: In an experiment, the control group is kept under normal conditions without the factor being tested, while the experimental group receives that factor. Comparing the two groups shows whether the results are really due to the tested factor or to some other cause. Without a control group, no reliable conclusion can be drawn from an experiment.

Q: iii. What deductions were developed during the study of malaria?

Ans: During the study of malaria, deductions such as these were developed: if Plasmodium lives in the blood of malarial patients, then it should be found in their blood; if mosquitoes carry Plasmodium, then malarial patients should have been bitten by mosquitoes; and if Anopheles mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium, then stopping mosquito bites should stop the spread of malaria. Experiments proved these deductions correct.

Q: iv. How Ronald Ross conducted the experiment to prove that mosquitoes are involved in the spread of malaria?

Ans: Ronald Ross allowed an Anopheles mosquito to bite a malarial patient so that it sucked Plasmodium with the blood. After some days he allowed the same mosquito to bite a healthy person (in his bird malaria experiments he used sparrows and Culex mosquitoes). The healthy subject developed malaria, and Plasmodium was found in the blood. In this way he proved that mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium and spread malaria.

Q: v. At what stage of the biological method, Hypothesis, is accepted or rejected?

Ans: The hypothesis is accepted or rejected at the stage of experimentation and analysis of results. After the experiments are performed and the data are analysed, if the results agree with the deductions, the hypothesis is accepted; if the results do not agree, the hypothesis is rejected or modified.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general statement.
  • Deductive reasoning moves from a general statement to specific deductions.
  • Induction helps in forming hypotheses, while deduction helps in testing them.
  • Laveran found Plasmodium in the blood of malarial patients.
  • Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • Mathematics removes personal bias and helps the biologist confirm, modify or reject a hypothesis.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Differentiate between inductive reasoning and deductive reasoning?

Ans: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general statement. For example, after observing many malarial patients, it was generalized that all malarial patients have Plasmodium in their blood. Deductive reasoning moves in the opposite direction, from a general statement to specific deductions: from the hypothesis "Plasmodium causes malaria" the deduction is drawn that Plasmodium must be present in the blood of every malarial patient. Induction helps in forming hypotheses, while deduction helps in testing them through experiments.

Q: ii. Explain how biologists use scientific method to solve the mysteries of addressing the malarial problem?

Ans: Biologists solved the malaria problem step by step through the scientific method. Problem: what causes malaria and how does it spread? Observations: Laveran found Plasmodium in the blood of malarial patients, and it was observed that malaria was common in marshy areas and among people bitten by mosquitoes. Hypothesis: Plasmodium is the cause of malaria and it is transmitted by mosquitoes. Deductions: Plasmodium should be present in the blood of all malarial patients, and it should also be present in the body of mosquitoes that bite them. Experiments: blood of healthy and infected persons was examined and compared; A. F. A. King and Ronald Ross performed experiments in which mosquitoes were allowed to bite malarial patients and then healthy persons, who developed malaria. Results supported the hypothesis, so it was accepted as the conclusion that malaria is caused by Plasmodium and spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

Q: iii. Explain that how mathematics can be used to interpret the data obtained through experimentation.

Ans: Mathematics is an integral part of the scientific process. Data obtained from experiments are organized in tables and graphs, and statistical formulae are applied to analyse them. Ratio and proportion are used to compare results, for example the number of infected and healthy persons, or the percentage of red blood cells destroyed by Plasmodium. lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Deforestation exposes soil to erosion, washes away fertile top soil and reduces rainfall, leading to desertification.
  • Classification makes the study of organisms easy and systematic and shows relationships between organisms.
  • Viruses are acellular particles of DNA or RNA in a protein coat and are kept outside the five kingdoms.
  • Monera are prokaryotic with no membrane-bounded nucleus, while Protista are eukaryotic.
  • Endangered species of Pakistan include the snow leopard, Indus dolphin, markhor and houbara bustard.
  • Habitat loss, hunting and poaching, pollution and over-grazing decrease endangered populations.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answer to the following questions

Q: i. How does deforestation lead to desertification?

Ans: Trees hold the soil with their roots and keep the climate moist by transpiration and rainfall. When forests are cut down, the soil is exposed to wind and rain, erosion washes away the fertile top soil, the land loses moisture and rainfall decreases. Gradually the fertile land turns into a dry, barren desert. In this way deforestation leads to desertification.

Q: ii. Why is it important for a biologist to understand biological classification?

Ans: Classification arranges the millions of organisms into groups on the basis of similarities and differences. It makes the study of organisms easy and systematic, shows the relationships between different organisms, helps in identifying new species and provides a basis for all other branches of biology. Without classification the study of biodiversity would be confused and impossible.

Q: iii. What is the status of viruses in classification?

Ans: Viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms of classification. They are acellular particles of DNA or RNA covered with a protein coat. They show living characters only inside a host cell, where they reproduce, and non-living characters outside the host, where they can even be crystallized. Therefore viruses are regarded as a link between living and non-living things and are kept outside the kingdom system.

Q: iv. How you can differentiate between kingdom Monera and Protista?

Ans: Kingdom Monera includes prokaryotic organisms: their cells have no membrane-bounded nucleus and no membrane-bounded organelles, e.g. bacteria. Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotic organisms: their cells have a proper membrane-bounded nucleus and organelles, e.g. Amoeba and Euglena. Monera are the simplest organisms, while Protista are comparatively more complex.

Q: v. List down the endangered species of Pakistan and what are the reasons behind their population decrease.

Ans: Endangered species of Pakistan include the snow leopard, Indus dolphin, markhor, houbara bustard, green turtle, vultures and the blackbuck. The reasons behind their population decrease are deforestation and loss of habitat, excessive hunting and poaching, pollution of land and water, over-grazing, and the expansion of cities and agriculture into natural habitats.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The two kingdom system placed fungi wrongly with plants and could not place Euglena properly.
  • The five kingdom system separates prokaryotes as Monera and gives fungi their own kingdom.
  • Man is classified as Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens.
  • Human activities such as deforestation, hunting, pollution and pesticide use reduce biodiversity.
  • Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-word genus and species name used worldwide.
  • Biodiversity is conserved through national parks, sanctuaries, anti-hunting laws and captive breeding.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Differentiate between two kingdom system and five kingdom system along their advantages and disadvantages.

Ans: In the two kingdom system of Linnaeus, all organisms were placed in only two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia, on the basis of the presence or absence of a cell wall and the ability to move. Its advantage was its simplicity, but it had serious disadvantages: fungi, which are non-photosynthetic, were wrongly placed with plants; Euglena, having both plant and animal characters, could not be placed properly; and prokaryotes and eukaryotes were mixed together. The five kingdom system of Whittaker (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) is based on cell structure, body organization and mode of nutrition. Its advantages are that prokaryotes are separated as Monera, fungi get their own kingdom, and unicellular eukaryotes are placed in Protista. Its disadvantage is that viruses still cannot be placed in any kingdom and the system is more complex.

Q: ii. Take one organisms and assign it to different ranks according to hierarchy of taxonomy.

Ans: Taking man (Homo sapiens) as an example, its ranks in the hierarchy of taxonomy are: Kingdom: Animalia; Phylum: Chordata; Class: Mammalia; Order: Primates; Family: Hominidae; Genus: Homo; Species: sapiens. Each higher rank includes more organisms with fewer similarities, while the species is the basic and smallest unit in which organisms are most similar and can interbreed.

Q: iii. How human activities affect the biodiversity of an area?

Ans: Human activities badly reduce the biodiversity of an area. Deforestation destroys the habitats of wild plants and animals. Hunting and poaching decrease the populations of wild animals. Industrial and domestic pollution of air, water and soil kills many species. Over-grazing, urbanization and construction of roads and dams convert natural habitats into farms and cities. The use of pesticides kills useful insects along with pests. As a result many species become rare, endangered or extinct and the biodiversity of the area falls.

Q: iv. Explain Binomial Nomenclature. What are its advantages?

Ans: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a scientific name consisting of two words: the first word is the name of the genus and the second word is the name of the species, e.g. Homo sapiens for man and Canis lupus for wolf. The genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter, and the name is written in italics. Advantages: every organism has one definite name all over the world; there is no confusion of local names which differ from place to place and language to language; the name shows the relationship of the organism with its genus; and scientists of all countries can understand and use the same name.

Q: v. What are the reasons for the extinction of biodiversity worldwide and what measures are required to conserve the biodiversity of Pakistan?

Ans: The reasons for the loss of biodiversity worldwide are destruction of natural habitats by deforestation, pollution of air, water and soil, over-hunting and over-exploitation of species, climatic changes, and the introduction of foreign species which compete with local species. Measures required to conserve the biodiversity of Pakistan are: protecting forests and stopping illegal cutting of trees; establishing national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and game reserves; making and strictly enforcing laws against hunting of endangered species; controlling pollution; breeding endangered species in captivity and releasing them in nature; and creating awareness among the people about the importance of biodiversity.

mcqs.why: The detailed answer lists this as a disadvantage of the Linnaeus two kingdom system, along with Euglena being unplaceable and prokaryotes and eukaryotes being mixed together.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Study a nearby ecosystem and record your observations. Develop links between the organisms that you observed.

Ans: Model study of a pond ecosystem. Observations: producers are green algae, Hydrilla and other water plants which prepare food by photosynthesis. Herbivores such as snails, insect larvae and small fish feed on these plants. Carnivores such as frogs and larger fish eat the herbivores, and birds like the kingfisher and heron feed on fish and frogs. Bacteria and fungi in the mud decompose the dead bodies of plants and animals and return minerals to the water, which are again used by the producers. Links: plants -> snails/small fish -> frog -> snake/heron form food chains, and all chains join into a food web. In this way every organism of the ecosystem is linked with others for food, and the decomposers link the living world with the non-living nutrients.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The cell theory states all organisms are composed of cells and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
  • Schleiden proposed the cell theory in 1838, Schwann in 1839, and Virchow added to it in 1855.
  • A simple tissue has one type of cell, while a compound tissue has more than one type working together.
  • The selectively permeable cell membrane controls exchange and maintains equilibrium of the cell.
  • Endocytosis takes materials into the cell, while exocytosis releases materials out of the cell.
  • Turgor pressure develops when water enters the plant cell by osmosis and the contents press on the wall.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: i. Who proposed the cell theory and what are the main points of the cell theory?

Ans: The cell theory was proposed by the German botanist Mathias Schleiden (1838) and the German zoologist Theodor Schwann (1839), and Rudolf Virchow added to it in 1855. Its main points are: (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the structural and functional unit of life; (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells by cell division.

Q: ii. Differentiate between simple and compound tissues.

Ans: A simple tissue is made of only one type of cells which perform the same function, e.g. parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma in plants. A compound (complex) tissue is made of more than one type of cells which work together for a common function, e.g. xylem and phloem in plants, which conduct water and food.

Q: iii. How cell membrane helps in maintaining equilibrium while exchanging materials with environment?

Ans: The cell membrane is selectively permeable, so it allows only needed materials to enter the cell and waste materials to leave it. By diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and active transport it controls the movement of water, salts, gases and food in both directions. In this way it keeps the internal composition of the cell constant and maintains equilibrium between the cell and its environment.

Q: iv. Differentiate between endocytosis and exocytosis.

Ans: Endocytosis is the taking in of materials by the cell: the cell membrane folds inward around the material and encloses it in a vesicle, e.g. Amoeba engulfing food (phagocytosis). Exocytosis is the removal of materials from the cell: vesicles containing secretions or wastes move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and release their contents outside, e.g. release of secretions by gland cells.

Q: v. How does turgor pressure develops in a plant cell?

Ans: The cell sap of the vacuole of a plant cell is more concentrated than the outside solution, so water enters the cell by osmosis. The swelling cytoplasm presses against the cell wall. The pressure exerted by the cell contents on the cell wall is called turgor pressure. It keeps the cell firm and turgid and supports the soft parts of the plant.

mcqs.why: The answer gives xylem and phloem as compound or complex tissues made of more than one type of cells working together for a common function, conducting water and food.

mcqs.why: The answer states the cell membrane is selectively permeable, allowing needed materials in and wastes out by diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and active transport.

mcqs.q: Which processes does the cell membrane use to exchange materials?
options: Diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and active transport
mcqs.why: The answer lists diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and active transport as the processes by which the membrane controls movement of water, salts, gases and food in both directions.

mcqs.q: Endocytosis is:
options: The removal of materials from the cell in vesicles
The taking in of materials as the membrane folds inward into a vesicle
The diffusion of water across a membrane
The release of secretions by gland cells
mcqs.why: The answer defines endocytosis as taking in materials: the membrane folds inward around the material and encloses it in a vesicle, for example Amoeba engulfing food by phagocytosis.

mcqs.q: Exocytosis is shown when:
options: Water enters a root hair by osmosis
Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release secretions outside the cell

mcqs.why: The answer defines exocytosis as removal of materials: vesicles with secretions or wastes fuse with the cell membrane and release their contents outside, for example in gland cells.

mcqs.q: Water enters a plant cell to develop turgor because:
options: The cell sap of the vacuole is more concentrated than the outside solution
The outside solution is more concentrated than the cell sap
The cell wall actively pumps water in
The cytoplasm loses water by osmosis
mcqs.why: The answer states the cell sap is more concentrated than the outside solution, so water enters by osmosis, the cytoplasm swells and presses against the cell wall as turgor pressure.

mcqs.q: Turgor pressure is useful to the plant because it:
options: Makes the cell flaccid and weak
Keeps the cell firm and turgid and supports the soft parts
Stops all osmosis in the cell
mcqs.why: The answer states turgor pressure keeps the cell firm and turgid and supports the soft parts of the plant, which is the benefit of the pressure on the cell wall.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Root hairs absorb water and minerals through a large surface area, thin wall and concentrated cell sap.
  • Xylem vessels are dead hollow tubes with lignified walls that conduct water and give support.
  • Meristematic tissue divides actively, while permanent tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
  • Xylem conducts water and minerals upward, while phloem conducts prepared food in plants.
  • Epithelial tissue covers surfaces, muscular tissue contracts for movement and nervous tissue transmits impulses.
  • Mitochondria release energy by respiration and chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Root hairs are adapted to absorption and xylem to support. Relate their functions to their structure.

Ans: A root hair is a long, thin, tubular extension of a root epidermal cell. Its large surface area, thin wall and absence of cuticle help it to absorb water and minerals from a large volume of soil, and its cell sap is concentrated so water enters by osmosis. Xylem vessels are made of dead, empty, tube-like cells joined end to end; their walls are thick and strengthened with lignin. The hollow tubes conduct water upward and the lignified thick walls give mechanical support and strength to the plant body. Thus the structure of both is fully suited to their functions.

Q: ii. Discuss different types of tissues found in plants. Elaborate your answer with relevant diagrams.

Ans: Plant tissues are of two main types. Meristematic tissues are made of young, actively dividing cells with dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei; they are found at the tips of roots and shoots (apical meristems) and bring about growth in length, while the cambium increases thickness. Permanent tissues are made of mature cells which have lost the power of division. They include simple tissues: parenchyma (thin-walled living cells for storage and photosynthesis), collenchyma (cells with unevenly thickened corners, giving flexibility and support) and sclerenchyma (dead cells with very thick lignified walls, giving strength). Compound tissues are xylem (tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; conducts water and minerals upward and gives support) and phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma; conducts prepared food). Diagram (in words): a section of a plant stem would show, from outside to inside, the single-layered epidermis, a region of collenchyma, a large ground region of rounded parenchyma cells, and vascular bundles in which xylem vessels appear as large empty tubes on the inner side and phloem as groups of small cells on the outer side.

Q: iii. Describe the nervous, muscular and epithelial tissues.

Ans: Epithelial tissue covers the body surface and lines the cavities and organs. Its cells are closely packed on a basement membrane; it protects the underlying parts and also performs secretion and absorption, e.g. skin and the lining of the gut. Muscular tissue is made of long muscle cells (fibres) containing contractile proteins; it contracts and relaxes to produce movement. It is of three types: skeletal (attached to bones, voluntary), smooth (in the walls of gut and vessels, involuntary) and cardiac (in the heart). Nervous tissue is made of nerve cells called neurons, each with a cell body, dendrites and a long axon. It receives stimuli and transmits nerve impulses, coordinating the activities of the body.

Q: iv. Write a note on the structures of cell wall, cell membrane, mitochondria and chloroplast of a plant cell.

Ans: Cell wall: a non-living, rigid layer outside the cell membrane, made mainly of cellulose fibres. It gives shape, protection and support to the plant cell and is freely permeable. Cell membrane: a thin, living, selectively permeable membrane made of lipids and proteins (fluid mosaic model); it controls the movement of materials in and out of the cell. Mitochondria: rod-shaped organelles covered by a double membrane; the inner membrane is folded into cristae and the inner cavity is the matrix. They release energy from food by respiration and are called the power houses of the cell. Chloroplast: a disc-shaped plastid covered by a double membrane, containing the green pigment chlorophyll in its thylakoid membranes arranged as grana, lying in a fluid called stroma. It is the site of photosynthesis.

mcqs.why: The detailed answer lists three types of muscular tissue: skeletal attached to bones and voluntary, smooth in walls of gut and vessels and involuntary, and cardiac in the heart.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Meiosis produces four haploid cells and creates genetic diversity in populations
  • If 2n = 8, a gamete after meiosis has n = 4 chromosomes
  • Chromosomes have the least amount of DNA at Telophase-II of meiosis
  • Crossing over occurs during Prophase-I of meiosis
  • Synapsis and crossing over occur in meiosis-I but never in mitosis
  • Meiosis takes place in the testes (and ovaries), not in lungs, heart or stomach
  • Regeneration takes place by mitosis, not by meiosis

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Encircle the best suitable answers

Q: i. All of the following are true for meiosis, EXCEPT:

Options: (a) There is no DNA synthesis between the divisions (b) The result is four cells with haploid number of chromosomes (c) Meiosis does not contribute to the genetic diversity in populations (d) Fusion of two products of meiosis produces a zygote

Correct answer: Meiosis does not contribute to the genetic diversity in populations

Q: ii. If 2n = 8, for a particular cell, then the chromosome number in egg cell after meiosis would be:

Options: (a) 12 (b) 10 (c) 8 (d) 4

Correct answer: 4

Q: iii. During which stage of meiosis do the chromosomes have the least amount of DNA?

Options: (a) Prophase-I (b) Prophase-II (c) Telophase-I (d) Telophase-II

Correct answer: Telophase-II

Q: iv. Which statement concerning both mitosis and meiosis is correct?

Options: (a) Meiosis produces 4 haploid cells while mitosis produces 2 diploid cells (b) Meiosis produces 4 diploid cells while mitosis produces 2 haploid cells (c) Meiosis maintains the number of chromosomes, while mitosis reduces it (d) Prophase-I of mitosis results in the formation of a tetrad but not in prophase-I of meiosis-I

Correct answer: Meiosis produces 4 haploid cells while mitosis produces 2 diploid cells

Q: v. During which phase of meiosis, crossing over occurs?

Options: (a) Prophase-I (b) Metaphase-I (c) Metaphase-II (d) Anaphase-I

Correct answer: Prophase-I

Q: vi. Which of the following occurs during meiosis-I but not during mitosis?

Options: (a) The chromatids of each chromosome are separated (b) Synapsis and crossing-over occurs (c) The nuclear envelope breaks down

Correct answer: Synapsis and crossing-over occurs

Q: vii. Meiosis takes place in which of the following organs?

Options: (a) Testes (b) Lungs (c) Heart (d) Stomach

Correct answer: Testes

Q: viii. Two sister chromatids are collectively called:

Options: (a) Chromosome (b) Centromere (c) Multichromatid (d) Homologous pair

Correct answer: Chromosome

Q: ix. During the process of regeneration, the type of cell division is:

Options: (a) Only 1st meiotic division (b) Both meiotic divisions (c) Mitosis (d) All of them

Correct answer: Mitosis

Q: x. Which of the following statements are true about homologous chromosomes?

Options: (a) They are identical (b) They pair-up during meiosis (c) One partner of homologous pair move to each daughter cell (d) All of them

Correct answer: All of them

mcqs.q: i. All of the following are true for meiosis, EXCEPT:
options: There is no DNA synthesis between the divisions
The result is four cells with haploid number of chromosomes
Meiosis does not contribute to the genetic diversity in populations
Fusion of two products of meiosis produces a zygote
mcqs.why: This statement is false, so it is the exception: the book's answers state that meiosis produces genetic variations by crossing over and random separation of chromosomes, so meiosis does contribute to diversity.

mcqs.q: ii. If 2n = 8, for a particular cell, then the chromosome number in egg cell after meiosis would be:
mcqs.why: Full working: the diploid number is 2n = 8, so the haploid number is n = 8 / 2 = 4. Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so an egg cell (a gamete) contains n = 4 chromosomes.

mcqs.q: iii. During which stage of meiosis do the chromosomes have the least amount of DNA?
mcqs.why: After the two meiotic divisions are complete at Telophase-II, each nucleus holds only the single haploid set with one chromatid per chromosome, so the amount of DNA per chromosome set is at its least.

mcqs.q: iv. Which statement concerning both mitosis and meiosis is correct?
options: Meiosis produces 4 haploid cells while mitosis produces 2 diploid cells
Meiosis produces 4 diploid cells while mitosis produces 2 haploid cells
Meiosis maintains the number of chromosomes, while mitosis reduces it
Prophase-I of mitosis results in the formation of a tetrad but not in prophase-I of meiosis-I
mcqs.why: The book's comparison states that mitosis gives two diploid daughter cells in one division, while meiosis gives four haploid daughter cells in two divisions; tetrads form in Prophase-I of meiosis, not of mitosis.

mcqs.q: v. During which phase of meiosis, crossing over occurs?
mcqs.why: The book's detailed answer places crossing over in the pachytene stage of Prophase-I, where chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata; it does not occur in any metaphase or anaphase.

mcqs.q: vi. Which of the following occurs during meiosis-I but not during mitosis?
options: The chromatids of each chromosome are separated
DNA is replicated before the division begins
mcqs.why: The book states that synapsis and crossing over occur in meiosis and never in mitosis. Note: the book prints only three options for this item, so a fourth option, DNA is replicated before the division begins, has been added here; DNA replication happens before both divisions, so it is a wrong choice.

mcqs.q: vii. Meiosis takes place in which of the following organs?
mcqs.why: The book's short answer states that meiosis takes place only in the germ cells of the reproductive organs, the testes and ovaries, for the formation of sperms and eggs; lungs, heart and stomach are body organs where it does not occur.

mcqs.q: viii. Two sister chromatids are collectively called:
mcqs.why: After the S phase each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, and the pair together is still called one chromosome, as stated in the book's description of interphase.

mcqs.q: ix. During the process of regeneration, the type of cell division is:
mcqs.why: Regeneration replaces lost parts with cells exactly like the parent cells, which is the work of mitosis in the book's answers. Note: the book's fourth option was a combined catch-all choice; it has been replaced here with Only 2nd meiotic division, a distinct wrong option, because regeneration is by mitosis alone.

mcqs.q: x. Which of the following statements are true about homologous chromosomes?
options: They pair-up during meiosis, one partner of each pair moves to each daughter cell, and the two partners carry genes for the same characters
One partner of homologous pair move to each daughter cell
mcqs.why: The book keys the combined statement as correct, so the combined choice is spelled out explicitly here in place of the book's combined option: homologous chromosomes pair up in meiosis and one partner of each pair moves to each daughter cell, as described in the book's account of Meiosis-I.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The cell cycle runs from a cell's formation by division until it divides again
  • The cell cycle has two main phases: interphase and the division phase
  • Interphase has three sub-phases: G1, S and G2
  • Meiosis occurs only in germ cells of testes and ovaries to form gametes
  • Uncontrolled mitosis produces tumours and cancer
  • A chiasma is where non-sister chromatids join during Prophase-I

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: i. Define cell cycle and in how many phases it is divided.

Ans: The cell cycle is the series of events that take place in a cell from the time it is formed by division until it divides again into two daughter cells. It is divided into two main phases: (1) interphase, the long preparatory phase with G1, S and G2 sub-phases, in which the cell grows and its DNA is replicated; and (2) the division phase, which includes mitosis or meiosis (nuclear division) followed by cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).

Q: ii. In which type of cells, meiosis take place and why it is important?

Ans: Meiosis takes place only in the germ cells of the reproductive organs (testes and ovaries) for the formation of gametes, i.e. sperms and eggs. It is important because it reduces the chromosome number to half in the gametes, so that after fertilization the normal diploid number is restored in the offspring. It also produces genetic variations by crossing over and random separation of chromosomes.

Q: iii. How does normal mitosis ensure normal life?

Ans: Normal, controlled mitosis produces new cells exactly like the parent cell. It is responsible for the growth of the body, repair of wounds and replacement of worn out and dead cells, and for asexual reproduction in many organisms. If mitosis stops, growth and repair become impossible; if it becomes uncontrolled, tumours and cancer develop. So normal mitosis is essential for normal life.

Q: iv. Give at least four differences between meiosis and mitosis.

Ans: 1. Mitosis occurs in somatic (body) cells, meiosis only in germ cells. 2. In mitosis one division produces two daughter cells; in meiosis two divisions produce four daughter cells. 3. Daughter cells of mitosis are diploid like the parent cell; daughter cells of meiosis are haploid with half the chromosomes. 4. Mitosis daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent; meiosis produces variations due to crossing over. 5. Synapsis and crossing over occur in meiosis, never in mitosis.

Q: v. What is chiasma and what is its role in crossing over?

Ans: Chiasma (plural chiasmata) is the point at which two non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes join with each other during prophase-I of meiosis. At the chiasma the chromatids break and exchange their segments. This exchange of genetic material is crossing over, and it produces new combinations of genes, which is a major source of variation in the offspring.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In G1 the cell grows and makes new proteins and organelles
  • In S phase DNA is replicated and each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids
  • In G2 the cell grows further and checks the duplicated DNA
  • Prophase-I stages are leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis
  • In Anaphase-I homologous chromosomes separate and the number is halved
  • In plant cells cytokinesis forms a cell plate; in animal cells a cleavage furrow forms

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Describe various phases of interphase of cell cycle with diagrams.

Ans: Interphase is the longest phase of the cell cycle, between two divisions. It has three sub-phases. G1 phase (first gap): the cell grows in size, makes new proteins and organelles and prepares for DNA synthesis; the chromosomes are single thin threads. S phase (synthesis): the DNA of every chromosome is replicated, so each chromosome becomes double, consisting of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere; the amount of DNA is doubled. G2 phase (second gap): the cell continues to grow, makes the proteins and structures needed for division, and checks the duplicated DNA. Diagram (in words): draw a circle representing the cell cycle; the largest part of the circle is marked interphase and divided into three arcs labelled G1, S and G2, and the remaining small arc is marked M phase (division). A second sketch shows a cell in interphase as a rounded cell with an intact nucleus containing a chromatin network, labelled: nucleus, chromatin, cytoplasm and cell membrane.

Q: ii. Discuss different events of Meiosis 1 with the help of diagrams.

Ans: Meiosis-I is the reduction division. Prophase-I is long and has five stages: in leptotene the chromosomes appear as thin threads; in zygotene homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) forming bivalents; in pachytene each bivalent has four chromatids (tetrad) and crossing over occurs at chiasmata; in diplotene the homologous chromosomes begin to separate but remain joined at chiasmata; in diakinesis the chromosomes become short and thick and the nuclear membrane disappears. Metaphase-I: the bivalents arrange themselves on the equator of the spindle. Anaphase-I: the homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles, so the chromosome number is halved. Telophase-I: two nuclei are formed, followed by cytokinesis, producing two haploid cells. Diagram (in words): draw four panels. Panel 1 (prophase-I): a cell whose nucleus contains two pairs of homologous chromosomes shown as X-shaped bodies paired side by side, with an exchange of segments marked between two chromatids. Panel 2 (metaphase-I): the paired chromosomes lined up in the middle of the cell on spindle fibres drawn from two poles. Panel 3 (anaphase-I): one chromosome of each pair moving towards each pole. Panel 4 (telophase-I): two separate cells, each containing half the number of chromosomes.

Q: iii. Explain different stage of mitosis with diagrams and at what stage, cytokinesis takes place?

Ans: Mitosis has four stages. Prophase: the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids; the nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear and spindle fibres form. Metaphase: the chromosomes arrange themselves in a single row on the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres. Anaphase: the sister chromatids separate at the centromeres and move to opposite poles, so each pole receives the full diploid set. Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil into chromatin, and a new nuclear membrane forms around each set, producing two nuclei. Cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm, begins during late anaphase/telophase: in animal cells a cleavage furrow pinches the cell into two, while in plant cells a cell plate forms in the middle. Diagram (in words): draw a row of four cells labelled prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase: in the first, thick X-shaped chromosomes are scattered in the cell; in the second, they are lined up in one row at the centre; in the third, V-shaped chromatids are moving apart towards the two poles; in the fourth, two new nuclei are present and the cell is pinching into two daughter cells.

options: The cell grows in size and makes new proteins and organelles
Sister chromatids move to opposite poles
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in G1, the first gap phase, the cell grows in size, makes new proteins and organelles and prepares for DNA synthesis, while chromosomes are single thin threads.

mcqs.q: What happens during the S phase of interphase?
options: The cell checks the duplicated DNA
The DNA of every chromosome is replicated and its amount is doubled
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in the S (synthesis) phase the DNA of every chromosome is replicated, each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, and the amount of DNA is doubled.

options: The cell continues to grow, makes proteins needed for division and checks the duplicated DNA
The chromosomes pair up by synapsis
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in G2, the second gap phase, the cell continues to grow, makes the proteins and structures needed for division, and checks the duplicated DNA.

mcqs.why: Exercise C lists the five stages of Prophase-I and states that in leptotene the chromosomes appear as thin threads, the first visible stage of Meiosis-I.

options: Homologous chromosomes pair up by synapsis, forming bivalents
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in zygotene the homologous chromosomes pair up, which is synapsis, forming bivalents; separation begins later, in diplotene.

options: A single chromosome with one chromatid
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in pachytene each bivalent has four chromatids, which is called a tetrad, and crossing over occurs between its chromatids at chiasmata.

mcqs.q: What happens during Metaphase-I of meiosis?
options: The bivalents arrange themselves on the equator of the spindle
Sister chromatids separate at the centromere
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in Metaphase-I the bivalents, the paired homologous chromosomes, arrange themselves on the equator of the spindle before separating in Anaphase-I.

mcqs.q: Why is Meiosis-I called the reduction division?
options: Because the cell becomes smaller in size
Because in Anaphase-I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles, halving the chromosome number
Because DNA is reduced in the S phase
Because only one daughter cell is produced
mcqs.why: Exercise C calls Meiosis-I the reduction division because in Anaphase-I the homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles, so the chromosome number is halved in the resulting cells.

mcqs.q: What happens in the metaphase stage of mitosis?
options: Chromosomes arrange in a single row on the equator, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres
A cell plate forms in the middle
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that in metaphase of mitosis the chromosomes arrange themselves in a single row on the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres.

mcqs.q: How does cytokinesis take place in a plant cell?
options: A cleavage furrow pinches the cell into two
A cell plate forms in the middle of the cell
The spindle fibres pull the cytoplasm apart
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that cytokinesis begins during late anaphase and telophase: in animal cells a cleavage furrow pinches the cell into two, while in plant cells a cell plate forms in the middle.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Enzymes are proteins that act as catalysts inside living bodies
  • Enzymes alter the rate of chemical reactions; they are not used up
  • Enzyme rate rises with temperature up to a maximum of about 40 degrees C
  • Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction
  • Cofactors help enzymes in their activity, and vitamins can act as coenzymes
  • Trypsin works at an alkaline pH
  • At 104 degrees F body enzymes stop working, which makes it critical

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Encircle the best suitable answers

Q: i. The chemicals which are involved as catalysts inside the living bodies are:

Options: (a) Carbohydrates (b) Fats (c) Proteins (d) Starch

Correct answer: Proteins

Q: ii. Enzymes are biological catalysts which:

Options: (a) Allow new chemical reactions to occur (b) Are used up during chemical reactions (c) Alter the direction of chemical reactions (d) Alter the rate of chemical reactions

Correct answer: Alter the rate of chemical reactions

Q: iii. The graph below shows that the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, its rate: (Diagram in words: the graph plots the rate of an enzyme catalysed reaction on the vertical axis against temperature on the horizontal axis; the curve starts at 0 degree C, rises steadily to a peak at 40 degree C, and then falls as temperature increases further.)

Options: (a) Increases when the temperature is increased (b) Decreases when the temperature is increased (c) Increases with temperature upto a maximum of 40 degree C (d) remain unchanged

Correct answer: Increases with temperature upto a maximum of 40 degree C

Q: iv. What is TRUE about enzymes?

Options: (a) All parts of enzyme molecule take part in reaction (b) Enzymes lower the activation energy of reaction (c) An enzyme can act upon any kind of substrates (d) They are needed in large quantities

Correct answer: Enzymes lower the activation energy of reaction

Q: v. What is TRUE about cofactors?

Options: (a) Take part in reactions (b) Help enzymes in their activity (c) Increase activation energy (d) Are composed of proteins

Correct answer: Help enzymes in their activity

Q: vi. One of the following may function as coenzymes for the enzymes:

Options: (a) Proteins (b) Carbohydrates (c) Vitamins (d) DNA

Correct answer: Vitamins

Q: vii. Increase or decrease in temperature beyond the optimum temperature will:

Options: (a) Increase the rate of reaction (b) Decrease the rate of reaction (c) Not affect the rate of reaction (d) Denature the enzyme

Correct answer: Decrease the rate of reaction

Q: viii. Trypsin, an enzymes, works at:

Options: (a) alkaline pH (b) acidic pH (c) neutral pH (d) pH does not affect its activity

Correct answer: alkaline pH

Q: ix. Change in environmental factors will affect enzymes activity and therefore, may affect:

Options: (a) Metabolism (b) Respiration (c) Digestion (d) All of them

Correct answer: All of them

Q: x. The body temperature at 104 degree F is known as critical because it causes:

Options: (a) Nerves breakdown (b) Boiling of body water (c) Enzymes stop to work (d) None of them

Correct answer: Enzymes stop to work

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The lock and key model was proposed by Emil Fischer; its active site is rigid
  • The induced-fit model was proposed by Daniel Koshland; its active site is flexible
  • An enzyme speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy
  • Denaturation destroys the active site's shape and the enzyme loses activity permanently
  • Each enzyme is specific: amylase acts only on starch, proteases only on proteins
  • Optimum temperature for human enzymes is about 37 degrees C; pepsin optimum pH is about 2 and trypsin about 8

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: i. Differentiate between lock and key model and the induced-fit model.

Ans: In the lock and key model (proposed by Emil Fischer), the active site of the enzyme is rigid and has a fixed shape exactly complementary to the substrate, just as a lock fits only one key. In the induced-fit model (proposed by Daniel Koshland), the active site is flexible; when the substrate comes near, the enzyme changes the shape of its active site slightly so that it fits the substrate properly. The induced-fit model is the more accepted explanation of enzyme action.

Q: ii. In what way does an enzyme affect the chemical reaction it catalyses?

Ans: An enzyme speeds up the chemical reaction by lowering its activation energy, the minimum energy needed to start the reaction. The enzyme itself is not used up or changed in the reaction and does not change the direction or the final products of the reaction; it only increases its rate, so the products are formed much faster.

Q: iii. What will be the effect on digestion if we take some digestive enzymes from outsides?

Ans: Digestive enzymes taken from outside (as medicines or supplements) help the body in breaking down food. They assist the body's own enzymes, so digestion becomes faster and more complete and problems like indigestion and heaviness are reduced. However, they only help digestion of food in the gut; they do not replace the enzymes working inside the cells.

Q: iv. What is meant by denaturation of enzyme?

Ans: Denaturation is the loss of the natural three-dimensional structure of an enzyme protein due to high temperature or extreme pH. The shape of the active site is destroyed, so the substrate can no longer fit into it and the enzyme loses its activity permanently. For example, body enzymes stop working when the temperature rises to about 104 degree F.

Q: v. How are enzymes specific for the substrate?

Ans: Every enzyme has an active site of a specific shape, made of a specific arrangement of amino acids. Only a substrate whose shape is complementary to that active site can fit into it and form an enzyme-substrate complex, like a key fitting a particular lock. Therefore each enzyme can act on only one substrate or one type of reaction; for example, amylase acts only on starch and proteases act only on proteins.

Q: vi. What are the terms used to describe the temperature and the pH at which an enzyme can work most effectively in a reaction?

Ans: The temperature at which an enzyme works most effectively is called its optimum temperature (about 37 degree C for human body enzymes). The pH at which an enzyme works most effectively is called its optimum pH, e.g. about pH 2 for pepsin of the stomach and about pH 8 for trypsin of the small intestine.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the lock and key model of enzyme action?
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that the lock and key model was proposed by Emil Fischer, in which the active site is rigid with a fixed shape exactly complementary to the substrate.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the induced-fit model of enzyme action?
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that the induced-fit model was proposed by Daniel Koshland, and that this model is the more accepted explanation of enzyme action.

mcqs.q: In the induced-fit model, what happens when the substrate comes near the enzyme?
options: The substrate changes its own shape permanently
The enzyme changes the shape of its active site slightly so it fits the substrate properly
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that in the induced-fit model the active site is flexible, and when the substrate comes near, the enzyme changes the shape of its active site slightly so that it fits the substrate properly.

mcqs.q: How does an enzyme affect the reaction it catalyses?
options: It lowers the activation energy, the minimum energy needed to start the reaction
It changes the final products of the reaction
It is used up so the reaction can finish
It reverses the direction of the reaction
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that an enzyme speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy, while itself remaining unchanged and not altering the direction or final products.

mcqs.q: What do digestive enzymes taken from outside the body do?
options: They replace the enzymes working inside the cells
They stop the body's own enzymes from working
They help break down food in the gut, so digestion becomes faster and more complete
They digest the walls of the stomach
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that digestive enzymes taken from outside assist the body's own enzymes so digestion becomes faster and more complete, but they do not replace the enzymes working inside the cells.

mcqs.q: What is denaturation of an enzyme?
options: The joining of an enzyme with its substrate
The loss of the enzyme's natural three-dimensional structure, destroying the active site's shape
The making of new enzymes by the cell
The lowering of activation energy by an enzyme
mcqs.why: Exercise B defines denaturation as the loss of the natural three-dimensional structure of an enzyme protein due to high temperature or extreme pH, so the substrate can no longer fit and activity is lost permanently.

mcqs.q: At about what body temperature do body enzymes stop working, as given in Exercise B?
mcqs.why: Exercise B gives this example of denaturation: body enzymes stop working when the temperature rises to about 104 degrees F, because the heat destroys their structure.

mcqs.q: Which example of enzyme specificity is given in Exercise B?
options: Lipase acts on starch and proteins
One enzyme acts on every substrate
Amylase acts only on starch and proteases act only on proteins
mcqs.why: Exercise B explains specificity with this example: each enzyme acts on only one substrate or one type of reaction, so amylase acts only on starch and proteases act only on proteins.

mcqs.q: What is the optimum temperature for human body enzymes?
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that the temperature at which an enzyme works most effectively is its optimum temperature, which is about 37 degrees C for human body enzymes.

mcqs.q: What is the optimum pH of trypsin?
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that the optimum pH of trypsin of the small intestine is about 8, while the optimum pH of pepsin of the stomach is about 2.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Rate rises with substrate concentration until all active sites are occupied, then stays constant
  • Many enzymes need cofactors or coenzymes; their absence lowers the rate
  • The enzyme is released unchanged at the end and can be used again and again
  • In the diagram, A is the substrate, B is the enzyme and C is the products
  • From 25 to 35 degrees C the rate increases; from 40 to 60 degrees C it falls as the enzyme denatures
  • Pepsin's optimum pH is about 2 and pancreatic lipase's optimum pH is about 8

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Describe the factors which affect the enzymes activities.

Ans: The main factors affecting enzyme activity are: (1) Temperature: the rate increases with temperature up to the optimum temperature (about 37-40 degree C) and then falls rapidly because the enzyme is denatured by heat. (2) pH: every enzyme works best at its optimum pH; change of pH on either side decreases its activity and may denature it. (3) Substrate concentration: the rate increases as substrate concentration increases, until all active sites are occupied, after which the rate becomes constant. (4) Enzyme concentration: the rate increases in proportion to the amount of enzyme, provided substrate is in excess. (5) Cofactors and coenzymes: many enzymes need metal ions or vitamins for their activity, and their absence lowers the rate.

Q: ii. Explain the mode of action of an enzyme in a reaction.

Ans: An enzyme acts through its active site. The substrate binds to the active site forming an enzyme-substrate complex. According to the lock and key model the active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate, while the induced-fit model says the active site moulds itself around the substrate. Within the complex the enzyme lowers the activation energy, the bonds of the substrate are weakened or broken, and the substrate is changed into products. The products leave the active site and the enzyme is released unchanged, ready to be used again. In short: Enzyme + Substrate -> Enzyme-Substrate Complex -> Enzyme + Products.

Q: iii. Write the various properties of enzymes.

Ans: The properties of enzymes are: (1) they are proteins in nature (except a few RNA enzymes); (2) they act as catalysts and speed up reactions by lowering activation energy; (3) they are needed in very small quantities; (4) they remain unchanged at the end of the reaction and can be used again and again; (5) they are highly specific for their substrate; (6) their activity is affected by temperature and pH, and each enzyme has its optimum temperature and optimum pH; (7) they can be denatured by high temperature and extreme pH; (8) many enzymes need cofactors or coenzymes for their activity; and (9) they catalyse reversible reactions.

Q: iv(a). The diagram shows the relationship between an enzyme, a substrate and the products of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction. What is represented by the parts labeled A, B and C in the diagram? Diagram (in words): in the first panel, A is a chain of four small circles shown above B, which is a solid block with two notches on its upper surface; in the middle panel the circles are sitting inside the notches of the block; in the last panel the circles have separated into pairs, labelled C, and the block is unchanged.

Ans: A represents the substrate (the substance on which the enzyme acts). B represents the enzyme; the notches on its surface are its active sites. C represents the products formed from the substrate at the end of the reaction.

Q: iv(b). Name two properties of enzymes that are represented in this diagram. What will happen to the chemical reaction if the enzyme is removed?

Ans: Two properties shown are: (1) specificity - the substrate fits exactly into the active site of the enzyme, as a key fits a lock; (2) the enzyme remains unchanged at the end of the reaction and can be used again. If the enzyme is removed, the reaction will not take place at a useful rate (practically it stops), because without the catalyst the activation energy is too high for the substrate to be converted into products under body conditions.

Q: iv(c). What will happen to the rate of reaction if the reaction temperature is raised steadily: (i) from 25 degree C to 35 degree C, and (ii) from 40 degree C to 60 degree C?

Ans: (i) From 25 degree C to 35 degree C the rate of reaction will increase, because the temperature is rising towards the optimum temperature of the enzyme and the molecules collide more often and with more energy. (ii) From 40 degree C to 60 degree C the rate will decrease and finally stop, because above the optimum temperature the enzyme protein is denatured and its active site is destroyed.

Q: iv(d). What term is used to describe the condition of the enzyme when it is heated to a temperature of 60 degree C and above?

Ans: The enzyme is said to be denatured. Its protein structure and the shape of its active site are destroyed by heat, so it permanently loses its catalytic activity.

Q: vi(A). The graph below shows the rate of an enzymatic reaction. According to graph A, at which temperature the enzyme activity is highest. When temperature increases above this point, what will happen to the enzyme? Diagram (in words): Graph A plots the rate of an enzyme catalysed reaction against temperature from 0 to 60 degree C; the curve rises from zero to a peak at about 37-40 degree C and then falls steeply to zero.

Ans: According to graph A the enzyme activity is highest at about 37-40 degree C, which is its optimum temperature. When the temperature increases above this point, the activity falls rapidly and the enzyme is denatured: its structure is destroyed and it stops working.

Q: vi(B). According to graph B, what is the optimum pH for (i) pepsin, and (ii) lipase? As pH moves away from the optimum value, what will happen to the enzyme activity? Diagram (in words): Graph B plots the rate of enzyme catalysed reaction against pH from 0 to 12; it has two bell-shaped curves, one labelled pepsin with its peak at about pH 2, and one labelled pancreatic lipase with its peak at about pH 8.

Ans: (i) The optimum pH for pepsin is about 2 (strongly acidic, as in the stomach). (ii) The optimum pH for pancreatic lipase is about 8 (alkaline, as in the small intestine). As the pH moves away from the optimum value on either side, the enzyme activity decreases, because the shape and charge of the active site change and the substrate no longer fits properly.

mcqs.q: What happens to the rate as substrate concentration keeps increasing?
options: It rises until all active sites are occupied, after which the rate becomes constant
It keeps rising without any limit
It falls from the very start
It stays constant from the very start
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that the rate increases as substrate concentration increases, until all active sites are occupied, after which the rate becomes constant because no free active site remains.

mcqs.q: How does enzyme concentration affect the rate of reaction?
options: More enzyme always slows the reaction
The rate increases in proportion to the amount of enzyme, provided substrate is in excess
Enzyme amount has no effect on the rate
The rate falls as enzyme amount rises
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that the rate increases in proportion to the amount of enzyme, provided substrate is in excess, because more active sites are available to work at the same time.

mcqs.q: What is the effect if an enzyme's needed cofactor or coenzyme is absent?
options: The enzyme works on other substrates
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that many enzymes need metal ions or vitamins for their activity, and their absence lowers the rate of the reaction the enzyme catalyses.

mcqs.q: What is formed when a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site?
mcqs.why: Exercise C describes the mode of action: the substrate binds to the active site forming an enzyme-substrate complex, within which the activation energy is lowered and the substrate is changed into products.

mcqs.q: What happens to the enzyme at the end of a reaction?
options: It is released unchanged, ready to be used again
It is denatured by the products
It becomes part of the substrate
mcqs.why: Exercise C summarises the mode of action as Enzyme plus Substrate gives the complex, then Enzyme plus Products: the products leave and the enzyme is released unchanged, ready to be used again.

mcqs.q: In what quantity are enzymes needed for a reaction?
options: In equal amount to the substrate
In amounts that grow with every use
mcqs.why: Exercise C lists among the properties of enzymes that they are needed in very small quantities, because each enzyme molecule is used again and again and is not consumed.

mcqs.q: Which kind of reactions can enzymes catalyse, according to their properties?
mcqs.why: Exercise C lists as a property of enzymes that they catalyse reversible reactions, speeding up the reaction in whichever direction conditions favour, without changing its direction themselves.

mcqs.q: In the enzyme diagram of Exercise C, what does the label A represent?
options: The substrate, the substance on which the enzyme acts
mcqs.why: Exercise C answers the diagram question directly: A represents the substrate, B represents the enzyme whose notches are its active sites, and C represents the products.

mcqs.q: In the enzyme diagram of Exercise C, what does the label B represent?
options: The enzyme, whose surface notches are its active sites
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that B represents the enzyme and the notches on its surface are its active sites, into which the substrate, labelled A, fits during the reaction.

options: The products formed from the substrate at the end of the reaction
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that C represents the products formed from the substrate at the end of the reaction, while the enzyme block in the last panel is unchanged.

mcqs.q: What happens to the reaction if the enzyme is removed?
options: It runs at the same speed
It runs faster without the enzyme
It produces different products at once
It does not take place at a useful rate, because the activation energy is too high under body conditions
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that if the enzyme is removed the reaction will not take place at a useful rate, practically it stops, because without the catalyst the activation energy is too high under body conditions.

mcqs.q: What happens to the rate when the temperature rises steadily from 25 degrees C to 35 degrees C?
options: The rate increases, as the temperature rises towards the optimum and molecules collide more often
The rate stays exactly the same
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that from 25 to 35 degrees C the rate increases, because the temperature is rising towards the optimum and the molecules collide more often and with more energy.

mcqs.q: What happens to the rate when the temperature rises from 40 degrees C to 60 degrees C?
options: The rate decreases and finally stops, because the enzyme protein is denatured
The rate doubles at 60 degrees C
mcqs.why: Exercise C states that from 40 to 60 degrees C the rate decreases and finally stops, because above the optimum temperature the enzyme protein is denatured and its active site is destroyed.

mcqs.q: According to graph A in Exercise C, at what temperature is enzyme activity highest?
mcqs.why: Exercise C reads graph A as peaking at about 37 to 40 degrees C, the optimum temperature; above this point activity falls rapidly and the enzyme is denatured.

mcqs.q: According to graph B in Exercise C, what is the optimum pH of pancreatic lipase?
mcqs.why: Exercise C reads graph B as showing pepsin peaking at about pH 2 and pancreatic lipase peaking at about pH 8, the alkaline conditions of the small intestine.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Dark reactions of photosynthesis take place in the stroma of the chloroplast.
  • Photosynthetic organisms trap light energy; photosynthesis occurs in mesophyll cells.
  • Pigments are not a limiting factor for photosynthesis; CO2 concentration, temperature and light intensity are.
  • Red and blue light are the important pair of colours for photosynthesis.
  • Oxygen may not be required for respiration, because anaerobic respiration proceeds without it.
  • In ATP the three phosphate groups are linked to ribose, and cells use ATP to carry out functions.
  • In a bacterial cell glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, and conversion of pyruvic acid to ethanol consumes one NADH.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Encircle the best suitable answers

Q: i. The site of the cell for the dark reaction is:

Options: (a) Mitochondria (b) Ribosome (c) Granum of chloroplast (d) Stroma of chloroplast

Correct answer: Stroma of chloroplast

Q: ii. The organisms responsible for trapping light energy are:

Options: (a) Plants (b) Algae (c) Photosynthetic organisms (d) Fungi

Correct answer: Photosynthetic organisms

Q: iii. Photosynthesis takes place in:

Options: (a) Mesophyll cells (b) Guard cells (c) Phloem cells (d) All of the above

Correct answer: Mesophyll cells

Q: iv. One of the following is not a limiting factor for enzymes in photosynthesis:

Options: (a) CO2 concentration (b) Temperature (c) Light intensity (d) Pigments

Correct answer: Pigments

Q: v. One of the following pair of light colours is important for photosynthesis:

Options: (a) Green and yellow (b) Yellow and orange (c) Green and orange (d) Red and blue

Correct answer: Red and blue

Q: vi. One of the following may not be required for respiration:

Options: (a) Oxygen (b) Food molecule (c) Enzymes (d) CO2

Correct answer: Oxygen

Q: vii. In the structure of ATP, the three phosphate groups are linked to:
