lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • ATP is the energy currency of the cell: energy from respiration is stored in ATP and released when ATP breaks down to ADP.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue and red light; accessory pigments absorb other wavelengths, pass energy to chlorophyll and protect it.
  • An ATP molecule consists of adenine, ribose and a chain of three phosphate groups joined by high-energy bonds.
  • Lactic acid fermentation converts pyruvic acid to lactic acid with no CO2; alcoholic fermentation converts it to ethanol and CO2.
  • Both fermentations begin with glycolysis, in which glucose is broken down into pyruvic acid.
  • In photosynthesis water is oxidized and CO2 is reduced to glucose; in respiration glucose is oxidized to release energy as ATP.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: i. Why is ATP regarded as the currency of the living cell?

Ans: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the universal energy carrier of the cell. Energy released from food during respiration is stored in ATP, and whenever and wherever the cell needs energy for its activities, ATP is broken down to ADP and the stored energy is released. Just as money is used for every payment, ATP is used for every energy need of the cell, so it is called the energy currency of the living cell.

Q: ii. What is the role of pigments during photosynthesis?

Ans: Photosynthetic pigments, mainly chlorophyll, absorb sunlight and convert light energy into chemical energy. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly the blue and red portions of light. The accessory pigments (carotenoids and xanthophylls) absorb other wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll, and also protect it. Without pigments, light energy cannot be trapped and photosynthesis cannot start.

Q: iii. Draw the structure of ATP molecule.

Ans: Diagram (in words): an ATP molecule has three parts joined in a row. On the left is adenine, a nitrogen-containing double-ring base. In the middle is ribose, a five-carbon sugar, attached to the adenine. On the right, attached to the ribose, is a chain of three phosphate groups one after another. The bonds joining the last two phosphate groups are high-energy bonds; when the terminal bond is broken, ATP changes into ADP and energy is released for the work of the cell.

Q: iv. Compare lactic acid fermentation with alcoholic fermentation.

Ans: Both are types of anaerobic respiration in which glucose is first broken down into pyruvic acid by glycolysis. In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvic acid is reduced into lactic acid; it occurs in muscles during vigorous exercise and in lactic acid bacteria, and no CO2 is produced. In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvic acid is converted into ethyl alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide is released; it occurs in yeast and is used in baking and in the making of beverages.

Q: v. Why are oxidation and reduction important for plants?

Ans: Oxidation (loss of hydrogen or electrons) and reduction (gain of hydrogen or electrons) are the basis of both photosynthesis and respiration in plants. In photosynthesis, water is oxidized and CO2 is reduced to form glucose, storing light energy in food. In respiration, glucose is oxidized to release that energy as ATP. These redox reactions also build and break down many other substances, so the whole energy economy of the plant depends on oxidation and reduction.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O, using sunlight in the presence of chlorophyll.
  • Light reactions in the grana split water by photolysis, release oxygen and produce ATP and NADPH.
  • Dark reactions (Calvin cycle) in the stroma reduce CO2 with hydrogen from NADPH, using ATP energy, to form glucose.
  • A limiting factor is present in the least quantity and limits the rate; for photosynthesis these are light intensity, CO2 concentration and temperature.
  • Aerobic respiration yields a net 36 ATP per glucose, while anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per glucose.
  • Glycolysis gives 2 net ATP, the Krebs cycle gives 2 ATP, and the electron transport chain gives about 32 ATP.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Explain the mechanism of photosynthesis.

Ans: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from CO2 and water using sunlight, in the presence of chlorophyll, and release oxygen as a by-product: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. It is completed in two steps. (1) Light reactions, which take place in the grana (thylakoids) of the chloroplast: chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split (photolysis) releasing oxygen, and ATP and NADPH are produced. (2) Dark reactions (Calvin cycle), which take place in the stroma: CO2 is reduced by hydrogen from NADPH, using the energy of ATP, and glucose is formed. The glucose is stored as starch or used by the plant.

Q: ii. What is the concept of a limiting factor? What are the different limiting factors for photosynthesis?

Ans: A limiting factor is an environmental factor which is present in the least quantity (or is deficient) and therefore limits the rate of a metabolic process, although all other factors may be favourable. For example, on a bright sunny day CO2 may become the limiting factor for photosynthesis. The main limiting factors for photosynthesis are: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. If any one of them is in short supply, the rate of photosynthesis remains low even if the other two are increased; the rate rises only when the limiting factor is increased.

Q: iii. Why is aerobic respiration considered to be more efficient than anaerobic respiration?

Ans: In aerobic respiration glucose is completely oxidized into CO2 and water, and one glucose molecule yields a net gain of 36 ATP. In anaerobic respiration glucose is only partially broken down into lactic acid or into ethanol and CO2, and the products still contain much energy, so only 2 ATP are produced per glucose molecule. Thus aerobic respiration releases and stores about eighteen times more energy from the same amount of food, and that is why it is considered much more efficient.

Q: iv. Aerobic respiration generates more ATP molecules than anaerobic process. Which processes of aerobic respiration are responsible for this higher generation of ATP and how?

Ans: Aerobic respiration has three steps: glycolysis in the cytoplasm produces 2 net ATP; the Krebs cycle in the mitochondria produces 2 ATP directly but also produces many NADH and FADH2 molecules; and the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane oxidizes these NADH and FADH2 and produces the bulk of the ATP (about 32 ATP). Anaerobic respiration consists of glycolysis and fermentation only, so it stops at 2 ATP. The Krebs cycle and especially the electron transport chain, which require oxygen, are therefore responsible for the much higher ATP generation of aerobic respiration (36 ATP in total).

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Food passes in order through mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus.
  • Mechanical digestion is by the teeth chewing, the stomach churning food into chyme, and peristalsis pushing food onward.
  • Glucose and amino acids are absorbed into blood capillaries of the villi; fat products are absorbed into the lacteals instead.
  • Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets before lipase digests them into fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Fertilizer hazards include nitrates in drinking water, eutrophication killing fish, and damage to soil and food chains.
  • Malnutrition is too little or too much of nutrients and causes diseases such as marasmus, kwashiorkor and obesity.
  • Dietary fiber adds bulk, stimulates peristalsis and prevents constipation.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: i. List all parts (in order) of the human digestive system through which food passes.

Ans: In order, the food passes through: oral cavity (mouth) -> pharynx -> oesophagus -> stomach -> small intestine (duodenum, jejunum and ileum) -> large intestine (caecum, colon and rectum) -> anus, from where the undigested food is removed as faeces.

Q: ii. How is food mechanically broken down during digestion?

Ans: Mechanical digestion breaks food into small pieces without changing it chemically. It is done by the teeth in the mouth, which cut, tear, grind and crush the food during chewing (mastication); by the churning movements of the stomach muscles, which mix and squeeze the food into chyme; and by the peristaltic movements of the alimentary canal, which keep crushing and pushing the food onward.

Q: iii. How does the digestion and absorption of fats differ from the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates and proteins?

Ans: Carbohydrates are digested to glucose and proteins to amino acids; these are water soluble and are absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi, going to the liver through the hepatic portal vein. Fats are first emulsified by bile into small droplets and then digested by lipase into fatty acids and glycerol; most of their products are absorbed into the lacteals (lymph vessels) of the villi instead of the blood capillaries, and reach the blood later through the lymphatic system.

Q: iv. Enlist five environmental hazards related to the use of fertilizers.

Ans: Five hazards of fertilizers are: (1) excess nitrates wash into drinking water and cause health problems, especially in babies; (2) fertilizers running into ponds and lakes cause eutrophication, in which algal growth uses up oxygen and kills fish; (3) they pollute and damage the soil structure and kill useful soil organisms; (4) they enter food chains and harm animals and birds; (5) their manufacture and over-use contribute to air and water pollution.

Q: v. What is malnutrition? Why it is considered to be a health hazard?

Ans: Malnutrition is the condition in which the body does not get the required amounts of nutrients, either too little (under-nutrition) or too much (over-nutrition) of food components. It is a health hazard because it causes diseases like marasmus and kwashiorkor in children, weakens immunity against infections, retards growth and mental development, and over-nutrition leads to obesity, heart diseases and diabetes.

Q: vi. Discuss the role of dietary fiber in balanced diet.

Ans: Dietary fiber is the indigestible part of plant food, mainly cellulose. It adds bulk to the food and stimulates peristalsis, so the food moves smoothly through the alimentary canal and constipation is prevented. It helps in the regular removal of faeces, lowers the absorption of excess fats and cholesterol, and keeps the colon healthy. A balanced diet must therefore contain fiber-rich foods like vegetables, fruits and whole grains.

mcqs.q: What is eutrophication, as described in the fertilizer hazards?

Soil losing its structure and useful organisms dying
Fertilizers running into ponds and lakes, causing algal growth that uses up oxygen and kills fish
Chemicals entering food chains and harming birds
mcqs.why: The book lists as a fertilizer hazard that fertilizers running into ponds and lakes cause eutrophication, in which algal growth uses up oxygen and kills fish, separate from the drinking-water and soil hazards it also lists.

mcqs.q: Why is malnutrition considered a health hazard?
options: It affects only the teeth and causes no other disease
It is caused only by eating too much fat
It prevents constipation and improves immunity
It causes diseases like marasmus and kwashiorkor, weakens immunity and retards growth and mental development
mcqs.why: The book defines malnutrition as too little or too much of nutrients and states it is a hazard because it causes marasmus and kwashiorkor in children, weakens immunity against infections, retards growth and mental development, and over-nutrition leads to obesity, heart diseases and diabetes.

mcqs.q: What is dietary fiber and what does it do in a balanced diet?
options: Indigestible plant material, mainly cellulose, that adds bulk, stimulates peristalsis and prevents constipation
A digestible protein that builds muscles and repairs tissues
A vitamin that is stored in the liver and released when needed
A mineral salt absorbed in the large intestine with water
mcqs.why: The book states dietary fiber is the indigestible part of plant food, mainly cellulose; it adds bulk to food, stimulates peristalsis so food moves smoothly, prevents constipation, and helps regular removal of faeces.

mcqs.q: Which foods does the book give as sources of dietary fiber?
options: Butter, cheese and fried foods only
mcqs.why: The book states a balanced diet must contain fiber-rich foods like vegetables, fruits and whole grains, because fiber also lowers absorption of excess fats and cholesterol and keeps the colon healthy.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Over-nutrition causes obesity, heart diseases, high blood pressure and diabetes.
  • Excess cholesterol deposits in the arteries as atherosclerosis and may cause heart attack; excess vitamins A and D can be toxic.
  • Salivary amylase digests starch to maltose; pepsin digests proteins to peptides; pancreatic lipase digests fats to fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Water forms about 70 percent of the body and is needed for digestion, transport, excretion and temperature regulation.
  • The epiglottis closes the wind pipe during swallowing so food enters the oesophagus, not the trachea.
  • In a villus, blood capillaries absorb glucose and amino acids to the liver, while the lacteal absorbs fat products into the lymph.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Overtake of nutrition can lead to serious health disorders. Evaluate the statement by giving examples.

Ans: The statement is correct. Over-intake of nutrients (over-nutrition) is a form of malnutrition. Taking excess carbohydrates and fats causes obesity, which leads to heart diseases, high blood pressure and diabetes. Excess of cholesterol-rich food deposits fats in the arteries (atherosclerosis) and may cause heart attack. Excess of salt raises blood pressure. Excess of vitamin A and D, stored in the body, can become toxic and damage the liver and bones. Excess of proteins burdens the kidneys. So just like deficiency, overtake of nutrition also leads to serious health disorders, and only a balanced diet keeps the body healthy.

Q: ii. List down major enzymes in the human digestive system. Elaborate their role in digestion.

Ans: The major digestive enzymes are: (1) Salivary amylase (in saliva, mouth): begins the digestion of starch into maltose. (2) Pepsin (gastric juice, stomach): digests proteins into peptides in acidic medium. (3) Pancreatic amylase (pancreatic juice, small intestine): digests starch into maltose. (4) Trypsin (pancreatic juice): digests proteins and peptides into smaller peptides. (5) Pancreatic lipase: digests emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol. (6) Intestinal enzymes (intestinal juice): maltase converts maltose to glucose, and peptidases convert peptides into amino acids, completing digestion. In this way the enzymes of the mouth, stomach, pancreas and intestine together break carbohydrates, proteins and fats into absorbable forms.

Q: iii. Explain the importance of water in the human body.

Ans: Water is essential for life. It forms about 70 percent of the body and is the main part of blood plasma and cytoplasm. It acts as a universal solvent in which all chemical reactions of the body take place. It is needed for digestion and for the transport of digested food, oxygen, hormones and wastes. It helps in excretion of urea through urine, regulates body temperature by sweating and evaporation, lubricates the joints and keeps the skin and mucous membranes moist. Without water, the metabolic activities stop and a person can survive only a few days.

Q: iv. Explain the role of oral cavity and pharynx in the digestive system.

Ans: The oral cavity receives the food. The teeth cut, tear and grind it into small pieces (mechanical digestion). The three pairs of salivary glands pour saliva, which moistens and lubricates the food, dissolves some of it for taste, and its enzyme salivary amylase begins the chemical digestion of starch. The tongue tastes the food, mixes it with saliva and rolls it into a small ball called bolus, and pushes it back. The pharynx is the common passage behind the oral cavity; during swallowing it passes the bolus into the oesophagus, while the epiglottis closes the wind pipe so that food does not enter the trachea.

Q: v. Describe the structure of a villus, including the roles of capillaries and lacteals.

Ans: A villus is a finger-like projection of the inner lining of the small intestine; millions of villi greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Diagram (in words): draw a finger-shaped projection covered by a single layer of thin epithelial cells; inside it draw a network of fine blood capillaries and, in the centre, a wider blind-ending vessel, the lacteal, surrounded by tissue cells. Structure and roles: the thin epithelium allows digested food to pass quickly into the vessels. The blood capillaries absorb glucose, amino acids, water, minerals and vitamins and carry them to the liver through the hepatic portal vein. The lacteal absorbs the products of fat digestion (fatty acids and glycerol, re-formed as fat droplets) and carries them through the lymphatic system into the blood.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Water is absorbed through root hairs by osmosis.
  • Leaves are the source in pressure-flow theory, not a sink; roots, stem tubers and fruits are sinks.
  • Sucking through a straw resembles the pull that moves material through the xylem.
  • Platelets are formed by bone marrow cells and are responsible for blood clotting.
  • Group O blood can be transfused to a person of any ABO group.
  • The left ventricle has the thickest wall; exchange with tissues occurs in capillaries.
  • Pulmonary veins are the exception carrying oxygenated blood; veins have valves against backflow.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Encircle the best suitable answers

Q: i. Absorption of water molecules through root hairs is due to:

Options: (a) Active transport (b) Diffusion (c) Osmosis (d) Pressure flow

Correct answer: Osmosis

Q: ii. According to pressure-flow theory one of the following is NOT a sink:

Options: (a) Root (b) Leaves (c) Stem tubers (d) Fruits

Correct answer: Leaves

Q: iii. When you suck a cold drink using drinking straw, it resembles with:

Options: (a) Diffusion (b) Flow of material in xylem (c) Flow of material in phloem (d) Root pressure

Correct answer: Flow of material in xylem

Q: iv. The cells which form platelets are:

Options: (a) Erythrocytes (b) Leucocytes (c) Bone marrow cells (d) All of these

Correct answer: Bone marrow cells

Q: v. A person is transfused with a donor's blood group "O". His blood group may be:

Options: (a) A (b) B (c) AB (d) All of the these

Correct answer: All of the these

Q: vi. Which of the following chambers has the thickest walls in human heart?

Options: (a) Right atrium (b) Left atrium (c) Left ventricle (d) Right ventricle

Correct answer: Left ventricle

Q: vii. The exchange of materials between the blood and tissues occurs in:

Options: (a) Arteries (b) Veins (c) Capillaries (d) Arteries and veins

Correct answer: Capillaries

Q: viii. All veins carry deoxygenated blood except the one vein called:

Options: (a) Vena cava (b) Hepatic portal (c) Pulmonary (d) Renal

Correct answer: Pulmonary

Q: ix. Valves to prevent the backflow of blood are found in the:

Options: (a) Arteries (b) Veins (c) Capillaries (d) Arteries and capillaries

Correct answer: Veins

Q: x. Which cells of blood are responsible for clotting?

Options: (a) Platelets (b) Erythrocytes (c) Neutrophils (d) Basophils

Correct answer: Platelets

Q: xi. A patient with blood group A can be given the blood of group:

Options: (a) A or AB (b) A or O (c) A only (d) O only

Correct answer: A or O

Q: xii. Myocardial infarction is due to blockage of blood flow in:

Options: (a) Aorta (b) Pulmonary artery (c) Coronary artery (d) Hepatic artery

Correct answer: Coronary artery

mcqs.why: Blood in veins flows towards the heart under low pressure, so veins have valves to prevent its backflow; arteries carry blood under high pressure and need no such valves.

mcqs.why: The coronary arteries supply blood to the heart muscle itself; blockage of a coronary artery stops that supply and causes myocardial infarction, a heart attack.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A mature RBC has no nucleus or organelles, leaving maximum space for haemoglobin.
  • Transpiration is faster on a sunny day because temperature is high and humidity is low.
  • Air bubbles break the continuous water column in xylem and stop the transpiration stream.
  • Translocation moves prepared food through phloem from source (leaves) to sinks in both directions.
  • In pressure-flow, sugar loading at the source draws water in by osmosis and raises pressure.
  • Plasma is about 55 percent of blood; RBCs carry oxygen, WBCs defend and platelets clot.
  • Without water on a hot June day, plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Answer the following questions

Q: i. Why does a RBC lack cellular organelles?

Ans: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus, mitochondria and other organelles so that maximum space is available inside it for haemoglobin, the pigment that carries oxygen. The absence of a nucleus also gives it a biconcave shape with a large surface area for the exchange of gases. In this way the RBC is fully specialized for transporting oxygen.

Q: ii. Is the rate of transpiration higher on a sunny day or a rainy day? Why?

Ans: The rate of transpiration is higher on a sunny day. On a sunny day the temperature is high and the air is dry (low humidity), so water evaporates faster from the leaf surface and the stomata remain open in light. On a rainy day the air is saturated with water vapours (high humidity) and the temperature is low, so transpiration becomes very slow.

Q: iii. What would happen to transpiration stream if the air is injected in xylem vessels?

Ans: The transpiration stream depends on an unbroken, continuous column of water in the xylem vessels, held together by cohesion between water molecules and pulled up by transpiration pull. If air is injected, air bubbles (embolism) break the continuity of the water column, the pull cannot be transmitted, and the upward movement of water stops; the leaves above that point would wilt.

Q: iv. What is translocation of food in plants?

Ans: Translocation is the transport of prepared food (mainly sugars) in solution form through the phloem, from the leaves where it is made (the source) to the parts where it is used or stored (the sinks), such as roots, fruits, seeds and growing tips. It takes place in both upward and downward directions according to the need of the plant.

Q: v. What is transpiration pull? Describe the importance of transpiration in the life of the plant.

Ans: Transpiration pull is the pulling force created in the xylem when water evaporates from the leaves during transpiration; it pulls the continuous water column upward from the roots to the top of the plant. Importance of transpiration: it is the main force for the ascent of sap (water and minerals) to the leaves; it keeps the cells turgid; it cools the leaves and protects them from overheating; and it helps in the absorption of water and minerals by the roots.

Q: vi. How does the pressure-flow theory explain the movement of sugars though phloem vessels of a plant?

Ans: According to the pressure-flow theory, sugars are actively loaded into the phloem (sieve tubes) at the source (leaf). This makes the phloem sap concentrated, so water enters by osmosis from the nearby xylem, creating high pressure at the source end. At the sink (e.g. root or fruit), sugars are unloaded and used or stored, water leaves the phloem, and the pressure falls. Because of this pressure difference, the sap containing sugars flows in bulk from the source to the sink.

Q: vii. Describe the composition of human blood. What are the main functions of blood cells?

Ans: Human blood consists of plasma (about 55 percent), a straw-coloured fluid containing water, proteins, salts, food and wastes, and blood cells (about 45 percent) floating in it. The cells are: red blood cells (erythrocytes), which carry oxygen by haemoglobin and also carry CO2; white blood cells (leucocytes), which defend the body against germs by engulfing them and by making antibodies; and platelets, which help in the clotting of blood at wounds.

Q: viii. How are different blood groups formed. What is their practical implication in blood transfusion?

Ans: Blood groups are formed by the presence or absence of antigens A and B on the surface of red blood cells and the Rh factor. Group A has antigen A, group B has antigen B, group AB has both, and group O has neither; a person is Rh positive if the Rh antigen is present. In transfusion the donor's antigens must not clash with the antibodies in the receiver's plasma, otherwise the red cells clump (agglutination) and the patient may die. So group O is the universal donor and AB the universal receiver, and blood must always be cross-matched before transfusion.

Q: ix. If we don't take water the whole day in the month of June, what would be the effect on volume of plasma in blood?

Ans: June is a very hot month, so much water is lost from the body in sweat and urine. If no water is taken the whole day, the water content of the blood decreases, so the volume of plasma falls. The blood becomes thicker and more concentrated, blood pressure may fall, and the person feels thirst, weakness and dehydration; the kidneys produce very little, concentrated urine to conserve water.

Q: x. Write any four differences between xylem and phloem.

Ans: 1. Xylem transports water and minerals from roots to leaves; phloem transports prepared food from leaves to all parts. 2. Movement in xylem is mostly upward; in phloem it is upward and downward both. 3. Xylem conducting cells (vessels and tracheids) are dead at maturity; phloem sieve tubes are living. 4. Xylem also gives mechanical support to the plant; phloem does not give significant support. 5. Flow in xylem is driven by transpiration pull; flow in phloem is driven by pressure difference (pressure-flow).

options: So that maximum space is available inside it for haemoglobin
So that it can divide rapidly in the blood
So that it can engulf germs like white cells
So that it can help in blood clotting

mcqs.q: The biconcave shape of the RBC helps it because it gives:
options: A large surface area for the exchange of gases
The ability to clot the blood

mcqs.q: Why is the rate of transpiration higher on a sunny day?
options: Because the air is saturated with water vapours
Because the stomata remain closed in light
Because temperature is high and the air is dry with low humidity
Because rainfall increases evaporation from leaves

mcqs.q: Why does transpiration become very slow on a rainy day?

Because the xylem vessels become blocked
Because the leaves lose their stomata
Because the air is saturated with water vapours and temperature is low
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that on a rainy day the air is saturated with water vapours, that is high humidity, and temperature is low, so transpiration becomes very slow.

mcqs.q: What happens to the transpiration stream if air is injected into xylem vessels?
options: Air bubbles break the water column and the upward movement of water stops
The water column becomes stronger and rises faster
Root pressure pushes the air out and flow continues
The leaves start absorbing water from the air
mcqs.why: Exercise B explains that air bubbles, embolism, break the continuity of the water column, the pull cannot be transmitted, water stops rising and leaves wilt.

mcqs.q: The transpiration stream depends on which condition in the xylem?
options: A column of water broken into short segments
An unbroken, continuous column of water held together by cohesion
Active pumping by living xylem cells
High pressure generated inside the roots alone
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that the stream depends on an unbroken, continuous column of water in xylem, held together by cohesion and pulled up by transpiration pull.

mcqs.q: Translocation of prepared food in plants takes place through the:
mcqs.why: Exercise B defines translocation as the transport of prepared food, mainly sugars, in solution form through the phloem from the source to the sinks.

mcqs.q: Transpiration pull is created in the xylem when:
options: Sugars are loaded into the phloem at the leaf
The roots absorb minerals from the soil
The stomata close during the night
Water evaporates from the leaves during transpiration
mcqs.why: Exercise B defines transpiration pull as the pulling force created in the xylem when water evaporates from the leaves during transpiration.

mcqs.q: According to pressure-flow theory, what happens at the source end of the phloem?
options: Sugars are loaded, water enters by osmosis and pressure becomes high
Sugars are unloaded and pressure falls to zero
Water leaves the phloem and the sap dries up
The sieve tubes die and stop conducting
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that sugars are actively loaded at the source, the sap becomes concentrated, water enters by osmosis from xylem and high pressure is created.

mcqs.q: According to pressure-flow theory, what happens at the sink end of the phloem?
options: Sugars are loaded and pressure rises
Sugars are unloaded, water leaves the phloem and pressure falls
Water enters by osmosis and pressure rises
The sap flows back towards the leaves
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that at the sink sugars are unloaded and used or stored, water leaves the phloem and pressure falls, so sap flows from source to sink.

mcqs.q: What is the main function of white blood cells (leucocytes)?
options: To help in the clotting of blood
To defend the body against germs by engulfing them and making antibodies
To carry digested food to the tissues
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that white blood cells defend the body against germs by engulfing them and by making antibodies, while RBCs carry oxygen and platelets clot blood.

mcqs.q: Which blood group is called the universal donor?
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that group O has neither A nor B antigens, so it is the universal donor, while group AB, having both antigens, is the universal receiver.

mcqs.q: Clumping of red cells (agglutination) during transfusion occurs when:
options: The donor antigens clash with the antibodies in the receiver plasma
The receiver has no Rh factor in the blood
The donor blood contains too much plasma
The blood is stored for a long time
mcqs.why: Exercise B explains that the donor antigens must not clash with antibodies in the receiver plasma, otherwise red cells clump, agglutination, and the patient may die.

mcqs.q: If no water is taken for a whole hot day in June, what happens to the plasma?
options: Plasma volume increases and blood becomes thinner
Plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker and more concentrated
Plasma changes into red blood cells
Plasma volume stays exactly the same
mcqs.why: Exercise B states that water lost in sweat and urine is not replaced, so the water content and volume of plasma fall and the blood becomes thicker.

mcqs.q: How does the direction of movement differ between xylem and phloem?
options: Xylem moves food both ways; phloem moves water upward only
Xylem moves only downward; phloem moves only upward
Movement in xylem is mostly upward; in phloem it is upward and downward both
Both xylem and phloem move materials only downward
mcqs.why: Exercise B lists this difference: movement in xylem is mostly upward from roots to leaves, while phloem transports food upward and downward according to need.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The septum divides the heart so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix.
  • The tricuspid valve guards the right side and the bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left side.
  • Arteries carry blood away under high pressure; veins return it under low pressure and have valves.
  • The pulmonary artery is the only artery with deoxygenated blood; pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
  • Transpiration through stomata creates the pull for the ascent of sap and cools the leaves.
  • RBCs number about 5 million per cubic millimetre and contain haemoglobin.
  • AB blood cannot be given to a group A patient because B antigens meet anti-B antibodies and clump.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: i. Draw the internal structure of a human heart and show the blood circulation with the help of arrows.

Ans: Diagram (in words): draw the heart as a cone-shaped organ divided lengthwise into right and left halves by a thick wall (septum). Each half has an upper thin-walled chamber, the atrium, and a lower thick-walled chamber, the ventricle; the left ventricle has the thickest wall. Label: superior and inferior vena cava opening into the right atrium; tricuspid valve between right atrium and right ventricle; pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle with a semilunar valve at its base; four pulmonary veins opening into the left atrium; bicuspid (mitral) valve between left atrium and left ventricle; and the aorta leaving the left ventricle with a semilunar valve at its base. Circulation with arrows: body -> vena cava -> right atrium -> tricuspid valve -> right ventricle -> pulmonary artery -> lungs -> pulmonary veins -> left atrium -> bicuspid valve -> left ventricle -> aorta -> whole body. The right side carries deoxygenated blood and the left side oxygenated blood, and the two never mix.

Q: ii. Discuss the function of major arteries and veins.

Ans: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; they have thick, elastic, muscular walls and no valves (except at the exit of the heart). The aorta is the largest artery; it receives oxygenated blood from the left ventricle and its branches (carotid to the head, subclavian to the arms, hepatic to the liver, renal to the kidneys, mesenteric to the gut, iliac to the legs, and the coronary arteries to the heart itself) distribute it to all organs. The pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood, from the right ventricle to the lungs. Veins carry blood towards the heart under low pressure; they have thin walls and valves to prevent backflow. The superior and inferior vena cava return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium; the pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood, from the lungs to the left atrium; and the hepatic portal vein carries digested food from the gut to the liver.

Q: iii. Discuss transpiration and its importance for plants.

Ans: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapours from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. Water absorbed by the roots rises through the xylem as the transpiration stream, because evaporation from the leaves creates a transpiration pull, and cohesion keeps the water column unbroken. Importance: (1) it is the main force responsible for the ascent of sap, i.e. the transport of water and dissolved minerals to the leaves; (2) it helps the roots to absorb more water and minerals from the soil; (3) evaporation cools the leaves and prevents them from being scorched by sunlight; (4) it keeps the cells turgid, supporting the plant and keeping the stomata open for gaseous exchange. Excessive transpiration, however, can cause wilting, so plants of dry areas have adaptations to reduce it.

Q: iv. Describe the structure of blood and its importance.

Ans: Blood is a fluid connective tissue consisting of plasma and blood cells. Plasma is a pale yellow fluid (about 55 percent of blood) containing water, proteins (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen), salts, digested food, hormones, gases and waste products. The cells (about 45 percent) are: red blood cells - biconcave, without nucleus, containing haemoglobin, about 5 million per cubic millimetre; white blood cells - larger, with nucleus, fewer in number (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils); and platelets - small cell fragments which help in clotting. Importance: blood transports oxygen, CO2, digested food, hormones and wastes between organs; it defends the body against diseases through white cells and antibodies; it clots at wounds and prevents blood loss; and it regulates body temperature, water balance and pH.

Q: v. Can a person with blood type AB donate blood to a person with blood type A? Explain your answer.

Ans: No. A person with blood group A has antigen A on his red blood cells and antibody anti-B in his plasma. AB blood has both A and B antigens on its red cells. If AB blood is given to an A patient, the B antigens of the donor's red cells react with the anti-B antibodies present in the patient's plasma. The donor red cells clump together (agglutination), block the blood vessels and may cause the death of the patient. Therefore AB blood cannot be donated to a group A person; a group A patient can safely receive only A or O blood.
